analysis.one_liner: Creates a joint federal commission to set uniform safety rules for banks trading derivatives.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a single representative with no cosponsors, never got a committee vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a Federal Derivatives Commission made up of the heads of the Fed, SEC, FDIC, and other regulators, charged with writing common rules for banks and other institutions that trade derivatives — contracts whose values rise and fall with interest rates, currencies, or stock prices. It would have required stronger capital and disclosure, discouraged banks from actively trading derivatives using federally insured deposits, and set basic prudence standards for municipalities and pension funds that use derivatives. It also tightened bank insolvency rules so the FDIC could act faster when a derivatives-heavy bank fails.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers who stand behind federal deposit insurance, because the bill would have imposed stronger capital and expertise requirements on institutions trading derivatives with insured deposits. Municipalities and pension funds that use derivatives would have gained minimum prudence standards, and mutual fund customers would have gotten clearer warnings about derivatives risk.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the new commission to consider strong capital requirements — with attention to leverage ratios — to guard against risks posed by derivatives, and to discourage active derivatives trading by institutions with access to federally insured deposits unless management demonstrates adequate capital and technical capability [S3].

It instructs the commission to recommend minimum prudential practices for municipalities and pension funds that use derivatives, and enhanced disclosure to mutual fund customers about derivatives risk [S3].

A bank executive's lack of adequate technical expertise in derivatives could be deemed an unsafe or unsound banking practice, giving regulators a new enforcement tool, and foreign banks would need comprehensive home-country derivatives supervision to open US offices [S3].

The FDIC would get expanded recordkeeping authority over derivatives at undercapitalized banks and clearer power to act when a failing institution's contracts are transferred, aimed at protecting the deposit insurance fund [S3].
The bill directs the Fed chairman to push other industrialized countries toward comparable capital and supervisory standards for derivatives [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and financial institutions engaged in derivatives activities — especially large derivatives dealers — would bear the cost of tighter capital standards, expanded reporting, board-level internal controls, and possible restrictions on trading with insured deposits. The six federal banking and market regulators would split the new commission's budget.

drawbacks.text: The commission's rules would be advisory in practice: each regulator could decline to issue the uniform regulations if it finds them 'not necessary or appropriate in the public interest,' and its recommendations could be rejected with a written statement, so the framework might produce coordination meetings more than binding rules [S3].

The bill adds a seventh coordinating body on top of six existing agencies — Fed, OCC, FDIC, OTS, SEC, CFTC, plus Treasury — raising the risk of duplicated oversight and slower regulation of a fast-moving market [S3].

Its insolvency provisions expand the definition of qualified financial contracts and strengthen the treatment of master netting agreements in FDIC receivership and bankruptcy, which favors derivatives counterparties — generally large financial firms — over other creditors of a failed bank [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — uniform, vigilant oversight of a market where banks were piling into complex contracts with deposit-insurance backing — addressed a real gap, and the taxpayer and depositor protections outweigh the compliance burden on banks. But the bill is loosely drafted: its centerpiece commission can be bypassed by any agency that objects, and its bankruptcy-side provisions actually hand some advantages to derivatives dealers. It would have been a start on oversight, not a finished framework.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by one member with no cosponsors, split across three House committees and three subcommittees, and none of them ever acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Leach introduced the Derivatives Supervision Act of 1994 on January 26, 1994, and it was referred jointly to the House committees on Agriculture, Banking Finance and Urban Affairs, and Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].

In February 1994 it was referred to three subcommittees — Environment Credit and Rural Development, Financial Institutions Supervision Regulation and Deposit Insurance, and Telecommunications and Finance [S5].
No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled in the House, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with the bill dead [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Derivatives dealers and banks came out ahead: no uniform capital, disclosure, or trading standards were imposed, and regulators retained full discretion over how — or whether — to supervise derivatives.

for.name: Rep. James A. Leach
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was his sole sponsorship, with no cosponsors

against.name: House committees on Agriculture, Banking Finance and Urban Affairs, and Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to three subcommittees and never reported it, keeping it from any floor vote

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern appears in the record; it died in committee referral.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed uniform capital, disclosure, and expertise standards and could have discouraged active trading by institutions backed by insured deposits. Dealers kept operating under agency-by-agency supervision of each regulator's choosing when the bill died.

industries.industry: Federally insured depository institutions and credit unions
industries.note: Banks would face tougher internal-control and recordkeeping rules, and credit unions would be held to derivatives standards no less stringent than banks'. Institutions not active in derivatives would feel little effect.

industries.industry: Federal financial regulators (Fed, OCC, FDIC, OTS, SEC, CFTC)
